findings.reason: a worker following the plan would keep operands resident (already true), watch the 29.4 ms survive, and never learn that removing it requires the read to return a device-resident result the step consumes on device, which the section does not specify.
findings.text: §2 says "The memory copies are removed only if the read's operands stay resident on the device: the §1 bank holds them, and the steady-state read copies no operand between host and device", but the `solve-wall-breakdown` trace it cites states the opposite: "Not host transfers of the operands. The operands are device-resident traced arguments … so no per-call transfer appears in the step", and attributes the 29.4 ms to "the read returning host-side data inside the measured call" — the copies are the read's *output*, not its operands, so the stated mechanism removes nothing and done-when (2)'s "copy bytes are zero" cannot be reached by it

findings.reason: the sentence tells a node the Krylov tolerance is provably harmless, so a 1e-6 mismatch will be hunted as a Jacobian defect instead of the solver tolerance, or the matrix-free option will be chosen on a guarantee that does not hold.
findings.text: §3 says "A Krylov solve is converged to 1e-10 relative linear residual, tighter than the 1e-6 agreements below, so its tolerance cannot decide them", but a relative residual of 1e-10 bounds the relative error in the update only by κ(A)·1e-10, and no condition-number bound is stated for the 1,650-row Newton matrix, so a Krylov solve at that tolerance can still miss the 1e-6 agreement in done-when (1)
